passage: "Friday. Done. One hundred percent," Elizabeth said at Monday's stand-up in their Bengaluru office, tapping the table. The new payment screen was hers, and she said it like a fact. Two teammates exchanged looks; last month her "two days" had become nine. Salma, the team lead, didn't roll her eyes, and she didn't just write Friday on the board either. "Great," she said. "Give me a range. Best case, likely case, and what happens if the bank's test server goes down again?" Elizabeth paused. "Best, Friday. Likely... Tuesday. Worst, if the server dies, the Friday after." Salma wrote all three on the board and told the client Tuesday. Elizabeth looked relieved.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's "two days" become last month?
qa.a: Last month her two days had become nine.

qa.q: Why might Elizabeth look relieved at the end?
qa.a: Giving a range took away the pressure of her all-or-nothing Friday promise, so she no longer has to be perfect to avoid letting everyone down.

qa.q: What did Salma's approach avoid, and why is that wise?
qa.a: She avoided both mocking Elizabeth and blindly trusting her; asking for a best, likely and worst case turned the certainty into a plan the client could rely on.

qa.q: How might the two teammates who exchanged looks see the stand-up?
qa.a: They may feel relieved that the lead handled it fairly, since a realistic date protects everyone from last month's scramble.

grounding: Shows a team seeing a colleague promise fast delivery with total certainty, and a lead asking for a range and worst case instead of trusting or punishing.

passage:
"I'll have the whole audit report by Wednesday," Manjula said. "Easy."
"The whole thing?" Rakesh asked. "Forty branches?"
"I've done audits before. Trust me."
Rakesh leaned back. "Last time you said that, we missed the deadline and the client—"
"Rakesh," said Devika, the senior analyst, gently. Then to Manjula: "I believe you're fast. Help me plan it, though. If everything goes right, when?"
"Wednesday."
"And if two branches send their data late, like in March?"
Manjula frowned. "Then... Friday. Maybe Monday."
"What's the worst case?"
"If the northern branches don't reply at all, a week late."
"Okay," Devika said. "I'll tell the client Friday and flag the northern branches today."

qa.q: How many branches does the audit cover?
qa.a: The audit covers forty branches.

qa.q: Why did Manjula frown at the question about late data?
qa.a: Manjula's easy promise had assumed everything would go right, and the reminder of March suddenly made the risks feel real.

qa.q: Why is Devika's response better than Rakesh's?
qa.a: Rakesh brought up the past failure as a jab, which could make Manjula defensive; Devika asked for best, likely and worst cases, which kept respect and produced a safer date.

qa.q: How might the client be affected by Devika's approach?
qa.a: The client gets a realistic Friday date and early warning about the northern branches, instead of a Wednesday promise that might break.

grounding: Shows a team member promising fast delivery with total assurance, and a senior asking for a range and a worst case rather than mocking or trusting it.

passage: Looking back at my first year as a team lead, the thing I'm proudest of is how I handled Kashish. I'm Avni, and I inherited a developer who promised everything with total confidence. "Two days, boss. Guaranteed." The first time, I believed him and told the client. It took eight. The second time I was so annoyed I nearly took the task away from him in front of everyone. Instead I tried something my old manager used to do: "I trust you're good. Give me three numbers: best case, likely, and if something breaks." He laughed, then thought. "Two, five, ten." It came in at six. We still use the three numbers, and now he gives them before I ask.

qa.q: How long did the first task Kashish promised in two days take?
qa.a: The first time, the task took eight days.

qa.q: Why did Avni nearly take the task away from Kashish in front of everyone?
qa.a: After believing the first promise and letting the client down, Avni felt annoyed and embarrassed, and wanted to stop relying on his certainty.

qa.q: What did the three-numbers question do that punishment would not?
qa.a: It respected his skill while making him think about what could go wrong, and gave Avni a range to plan around; punishing him would only have hidden the problem.

qa.q: How has the approach changed things for Kashish?
qa.a: Kashish now gives the three numbers before being asked, which suggests he feels trusted and has started building doubt into his own estimates.

grounding: Shows a lead dealing with a colleague's total certainty by asking for best, likely and worst cases instead of punishing or blindly trusting him.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Rao Caterers kitchen, Tuesday. Written by Aparna.
Akash, our newest cook, told the team this morning that he would have all 600 sweet boxes for the Kulkarni wedding ready by Thursday noon. "No problem at all, I've done big orders." He said it with such certainty that two of the helpers started planning their Thursday off. I've seen this before, so I didn't argue and I didn't just nod. I asked him, "What's your best case, your likely case and your worst case?" He paused. Best: Wednesday night. Likely: Thursday morning. Worst: if the khoa delivery is late, Friday. Friday is too late for the wedding. So we ordered the khoa a day earlier and kept one helper on standby for Thursday. Akash looked a bit deflated at first, but later he told me, "I never think about the worst case. That was useful."

qa.q: How many sweet boxes did Akash promise for the Kulkarni wedding?
qa.a: All 600 sweet boxes, ready by Thursday noon.

qa.q: How did Akash feel after being asked for a worst case, and why?
qa.a: He looked a bit deflated at first because his confident promise was being questioned. Later he found it useful, since he had never thought about what could go wrong.

qa.q: What did Aparna do instead of arguing or blindly trusting Akash?
qa.a: Aparna asked for a best, likely and worst case. When the worst case showed a problem, the khoa was ordered earlier and kept a helper on standby.

qa.q: How might the helpers who had planned Thursday off see Akash's promise now?
qa.a: They may be a bit disappointed to lose the day off but relieved the team won't be caught short if the khoa is late.

grounding: A catering supervisor sees a new cook promise fast delivery with total confidence and asks for best, likely and worst cases instead of arguing.

passage:
Wednesday night
Today at the NGO meeting, Gopika said she'd translate the whole 80-page health-worker manual into Marathi by Monday. "Easy, I'm fast," she said, and everyone relaxed. I'm the team lead, and part of me wanted to believe her, because the funders are waiting. Another part of me remembered how long the last 20 pages took. I didn't want to embarrass her in front of everyone, and I didn't want to just say okay either. After the meeting I asked her over chai, "What's the fastest you could do it, what's realistic, and what could go wrong?" She laughed first, then thought. Fastest Monday. Realistic Thursday. Worst, if the medical terms need checking, two weeks. Two weeks! So I've told the funders "next Friday" and asked Rohini to check terms in parallel. Gopika seemed relieved, actually.
Sangeeta

qa.q: How many pages is the health-worker manual?
qa.a: It is an 80-page manual.

qa.q: Why did part of Sangeeta want to believe Gopika?
qa.a: The funders were waiting, so a quick, confident promise felt like a relief. Believing it would have made Sangeeta's own worry go away.

qa.q: What choice did Sangeeta make over chai, and how did it help?
qa.a: Sangeeta privately asked for the fastest, realistic and worst case. That revealed a possible two-week delay, so Sangeeta set a safer date and got Rohini to help.

qa.q: Why might Gopika have seemed relieved after the conversation?
qa.a: Gopika may have felt pressure from her own bold promise, and a realistic plan with help took that weight off.

grounding: A team lead's diary shows the lead asking a confident colleague for a range and worst case instead of trusting or scolding the promise.
